name: Kingdom of Prussia (Frederick II)

areaKm2.note: world_1715 Prussia (35,746 km2) + Brandenburg (70,231 km2) = 105,977 km2 on the sphere; Silesia and Glatz (~37,000 km2, annexed 1742), Swedish Pomerania south of the Peene (1720) and the western provinces (Cleves, Mark, Minden, Ravensberg, East Frisia ~15,000 km2) are not in those polygons. ~160,000 km2 total; the map border understates the state.

population.note: Showalter, The Wars of Frederick the Great (1996) ch. 4: Prussia had ~4.5M subjects in 1756 after the annexation of Silesia (~1M). Population convention: all Hohenzollern lands incl. Silesia, Cleves, Mark and East Frisia; the Swiss principality of Neuchatel excluded. Range covers estimates from 4.0M (older) to 4.9M.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share: Germany 9.8% (1750). Berlin ~126,000 with garrison. Mid 10%.

activePersonnel.note: Frederick opened the war with an army of ~150,000 (Prussian Army article; Showalter ch. 4 and Duffy, The Army of Frederick the Great give 143,000-154,000 incl. garrison regiments). Counted: field and garrison regiments incl. cantonists on furlough who belonged to the regiments (recalled each spring), artillery and engineers.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: garrison and depot battalions, and the Landmilitz and provincial militias raised from 1757 (Pomerania, East Prussia). Enrolled cantonists not yet called are counted here.

supportPersonnel.note: Field and garrison artillery (~5,000-6,000), pioneers and engineers, train, staff (Showalter ch. 4). No navy.

mobilizationRatio.note: Prussia kept ~3.3% of its population under arms in peace and mobilised ~250,000 at the war's peak with foreign recruits (Showalter ch. 4); ~6-10% ceiling under the canton system in total war.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Musketeer, fusilier and grenadier battalions and the Potsdam Guard plus garrison regiments; ~2/3 of 150,000 (Prussian Army article; Duffy, Army of Frederick the Great).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: iron ramrods (from 1718), standard 1740 musket, battalion guns

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: the best-drilled infantry in Europe: 3-4 volleys a minute, oblique order (Leuthen 1757)

count.note: Educated guess: Feldjager corps (~300 in 1756) and the first Freibataillone (from 1756-57).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: rifled jager carbines

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: Freibataillone of mixed quality

count.note: Cuirassier regiments (13 incl. Garde du Corps and Gendarmes, 5 squadrons each at ~850-900 men per regiment).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: big horses, reformed by Seydlitz and Zieten for charging at the gallop

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Rossbach 1757 showed their quality

count.note: Dragoon regiments (~12, ~15,000) and hussar regiments (8, ~9,000). Dragoons counted as light cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: dragoons used as battle cavalry; hussars on the Hungarian model

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Seydlitz/Zieten reforms after Mollwitz

count.note: Two battalion guns per infantry battalion (~100 battalions -> ~200) plus heavy 12-pdr and howitzer batteries; Showalter ch. 4. Fortress guns excluded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: light battalion guns, heavier Brummer 12-pdrs added 1759

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional but the least favoured arm under Frederick

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 1.0 (best-in-era). Evidence: Frederick II (Hohenfriedberg 1745, Rossbach and Leuthen 1757), with Schwerin, Seydlitz, Zieten, Prince Henry

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75-1.0. Evidence: cantonal regiments recruited from their districts, harsh discipline; foreign enlistees deserted more

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: victories of the Silesian Wars (1740-45)

weapons.note: Anchor: 5.85 near 6 (1805). Evidence: iron ramrod flintlock, battalion guns; close to the Napoleonic anchor

ships.note: Anchor: none applies. Evidence: Prussia had no seagoing navy in 1756 (a small Stettin flotilla was improvised in 1759); value 0 so the engine gives it no naval capability.

fortification.note: Anchor: 5.8. Evidence: modernised fortresses at Glatz, Schweidnitz, Neisse, Magdeburg

logistics.note: Anchor: 5.6. Evidence: five-day magazine system and Oder/Elbe river transport

communications.note: Anchor: 5.5. Evidence: courier post, no semaphore

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

air.note: No aircraft or military balloons before 1783/1794.

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Germany 1756 = 1,733 (Maddison Project 2023, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true); the Prussian heartland (Brandenburg, Pomerania, East Prussia) was poorer than western Germany. Mid ~1,550. No Prussian series in the MPD.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Showalter ch. 4: the army took ~70-80% of state revenue (~12-13M thaler) and Frederick held a war chest of ~13M thaler; British subsidies from 1758. Peacetime ~4-6% of GDP; wartime higher.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: Silesian linen, Berlin textiles and arms (Potsdam-Spandau rifle factory 1722).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: East Prussian and Pomeranian grain surpluses; state granaries (Magazinpolitik).

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: few made roads; Oder, Elbe and canals (Finow canal 1746, Plauen canal 1745) used for military supply.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Stettin and Konigsberg shipping.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-54657-5) ch. 1: 17th-18th c. armies tied to magazines and bread ovens, operating ~5 marches (~100-150 km) beyond the nearest magazine or navigable river; requisition extends it in rich country. Frederick's five-day rule kept armies within ~3-5 marches of a magazine.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: horses and oxen for ~4.4M people; the army needed ~50,000 horses.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: fortress chain in Silesia and on the Oder/Elbe, loyal population; open plains, no strategic depth.

notes: Snapshot = August 1756, invasion of Saxony opening the Seven Years War. Population and territory: all Hohenzollern lands incl. Silesia and the western enclaves; the world_1715 polygons (Prussia + Brandenburg) miss Silesia and the west, so the drawn border understates the state. Personnel convention: all regiments of the standing army incl. cantonists on furlough are active (they were enrolled soldiers recalled for the spring exercises); garrison militias and later Landmilitz are trainedReserves. No navy (ships omitted).
